chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi and Muawiya ibn Ammar and Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he
said regarding the man who emancipates the slave: He said: 'Indeed, God — Mighty and Majestic — will emancipate for every organ of his (the slave's), an organ (of the emancipator) from the Fire.'
He said: 'And it is recommended for the man to draw closer to God on the evening of Arafah and the day of Arafah through emancipation and charity.'

key_terms.الصَّدَقَة: Voluntary charity, given for God's sake
key_terms.الْعِتْق: Manumission, the act of freeing a slave — a meritorious deed in Islamic law
key_terms.الْمَمْلُوك: The owned/possessed one; a slave or bondsperson
key_terms.عَشِيَّةَ عَرَفَةَ: The evening before the Day of Arafah, the 9th of Dhul Hijja
key_terms.يَوْمَ عَرَفَةَ: The Day of Arafah, when pilgrims gather on the plain of Arafah

ai.seo_question: What reward does a person receive for freeing a slave according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) teaches the immense spiritual reward of freeing a slave: for each limb of the slave emancipated, God frees a corresponding limb of the emancipator from Hellfire. The Imam further recommends making the eve and day of Arafah — the climactic day of the Hajj pilgrimage — occasions for emancipating slaves and giving charity as acts of drawing close to God. This teaching was addressed to a community where slavery was legally recognized, and the Imam's encouragement of manumission was a consistent Shia emphasis on the merit of freeing the enslaved.
